subject: maths
title: Data and Graphs: Tally Marks, Pictographs and Column Graphs
seo_title: Year 3 Data and Graphs Worksheets: Tally Marks, Pictographs and Column Graphs (Free, with Answer Key)
standard_text: Create and compare different graphical representations of data sets including using software where appropriate; interpret the data in terms of the context
meta_desc: Free Year 3 maths worksheets on data and graphs for the Australian Curriculum: tally marks and frequency tables, pictographs with a key, column graphs with scales of 1, 2 and 5, comparing graphs and NAPLAN-style “how many more?” questions. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Read the key or the scale first. Then read every row or column.
key_sub: A tally group is 5. If one symbol = 2, half a symbol = 1. A column halfway between 6 and 8 shows 7. Altogether means add; how many more means subtract.
body_html:
Collect, then show the data

Data is information we collect, such as votes in a class survey. Some data is in categories (words, such as cricket or netball). Some data is numbers (such as how many people are in each family).

We record the data with tally marks, write it in a frequency table, then show it as a pictograph or a column graph. All four can show the same data.

Tally marks and frequency tables

Draw one mark for each answer. The fifth mark goes across the other four. Count the groups in 5s, then add the single marks. The frequency is how many.

Example

How many students chose netball?

1 group of 5 is 5. Then 2 more: 6, 7.

Answer: 7 students

Pictographs

Look at the key first. One symbol can stand for 1, 2 or 5. Count the symbols in 1s, 2s or 5s. If one symbol stands for 2, half a symbol stands for 1.

Example

How many students chose soccer?

2 circles. Count in 2s: 2, 4.

Answer: 4 students

Column graphs

Find what the scale goes up in: 1s, 2s or 5s. Go across from the top of the column to the scale. If a column ends halfway between two gridlines, the number is halfway between them.

Example

How many more students chose AFL than cricket?

AFL 8, cricket 5. 8 − 5 = 3.

Answer: 3 more students

The table, the pictograph and the column graph above all show the same data. To check that two graphs match, read every category in both.

Add or subtract?

The question saysDo this
altogether, in total, both, A or BAdd
how many more, how many fewer, differenceSubtract
Two-step example

Netball got 7 votes and soccer got 4. How many more votes did netball and soccer get together than AFL (8)?

Step 1: 7 + 4 = 11. Step 2: 11 − 8 = 3.

Answer: 3 more votes

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting a tally group of 5 as 4The line across is the fifth mark
Counting symbols and ignoring the key (4 circles = 4)Use the key: 4 circles of 2 = 8
Saying half a symbol = 1 for every keyHalf a symbol is half of the key
Reading a column between gridlines as the lower lineHalfway between 6 and 8 is 7
Counting grid spaces instead of reading the scaleRead the number on the scale
Adding when the question says how many moreHow many more means subtract

faq.q: What do Year 3 students learn about data in the Australian Curriculum?
faq.a: They collect data with tally marks, record it in frequency tables, and show it in pictographs and column graphs. They compare the graphs and explain what the data tells them.

faq.q: What is the difference between a pictograph and a column graph?
faq.a: A pictograph uses symbols, and a key tells you how many each symbol stands for. A column graph uses columns, and you read the height against the scale.

faq.q: How do you read tally marks?
faq.a: Each group of four lines with one line across is 5. Count the groups in 5s, then add the single marks: 3 groups and 2 marks is 17.

faq.q: Are graphs and tables in the Year 3 NAPLAN numeracy test?
faq.a: Yes. NAPLAN numeracy includes statistics, so students may need to read tables, pictographs and column graphs and answer questions such as “How many more?”.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 1 group of 5 and 3 more: 1 × 5 = 5, and 5 + 3 = 8.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 2 groups of 5 and 3 more: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 + 3 = 13.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 3 groups of 5 and 4 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 4 = 19.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 4 groups of 5 and 2 more: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 + 2 = 22.
16 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 1, so look for 3 groups of 5 and 1 single mark. That is B. A shows 21 (one group of 5 too many); C shows 15 (one single mark is missing); D shows 17 (one single mark too many).

items.q: What number should go in the Frequency column for Mango?
items.e: The frequency is the number the tally marks show. Mango has 2 groups of 5 and 4 more: 2 × 5 = 10, and 10 + 4 = 14.

items.q: Which fruit got the most votes?
items.e: Mango has 14 votes (2 groups of 5 and 4 more). That is more than Watermelon (11) and Apple (9).

items.q: How many more votes did Watermelon get than Orange?
items.e: Watermelon 11, Orange 4. How many more means find the difference: 11 − 4 = 7.

items.q: How many students voted altogether? (Each student voted once.)
items.e: Find the Mango frequency first: 14. Then add all the rows: 9 + 6 + 14 + 4 + 11 = 44.

items.q: How many families have 4 people?
items.e: Find the row for 4 people. The frequency is 11 (2 groups of 5 and 1 more). The 4 is the number of people, not the number of families.

items.q: Which number of people is the most common family size?
items.e: The biggest frequency is 11, in the row for 4 people. So 4 people is the most common family size. 11 is how many families, not how many people.

items.q: How many families are in the survey?
items.e: Add the frequencies: 3 + 7 + 11 + 5 + 2 = 28 families. (20 is 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6, the family sizes.)

items.q: How many families have more than 4 people?
items.e: More than 4 means 5 or 6 people: 5 + 2 = 7 families. Do not include the families with exactly 4 people.

items.q: How many more magpies than galahs were seen?
items.e: Magpie 12, Galah 8. How many more means subtract: 12 − 8 = 4.

items.q: Which bird was seen half as many times as the magpie?
items.e: The magpie was seen 12 times. Half of 12 is 6. The ibis has a frequency of 6.

items.q: Mia sees 4 more lorikeets. What is the new frequency for Lorikeet?
items.e: The lorikeet frequency was 15. 4 more means add: 15 + 4 = 19.

items.q: Which survey question has answers that are numbers?
c: How do you get to school?
How many pets do you have?
items.e: “How many pets do you have?” has number answers, such as 0, 1, 2 or 3. The other questions have answers that are words (categories), such as red, bus or cricket.

items.q: Which survey question has answers that are categories (words), not numbers?
c: How many brothers and sisters do you have?
How many people are in your family?
How many books did you read this week?
items.e: Favourite fruit gives answers like apple or mango. These are categories. The other questions ask “how many”, so the answers are numbers.

items.q: Jack makes a tally of the cars that pass the school gate. He draws 4 groups of five and 3 single marks. How many cars has he counted?
items.e: Each group of five shows 5: 5, 10, 15, 20. Then 3 more: 21, 22, 23. So 23 cars. (Counting each group as 4 gives 19.)

items.q: Ruby counted 17 votes for netball. How should she draw the tally?
items.e: 17 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 2. Draw 3 groups of five (four lines and one across) and 2 single marks. Never leave 5 or more single marks: make another group of five.

items.q: How many students have a fish?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 1 student. The Fish row has 8 circles, so it shows 8 students.
Every star stands for the same number, so the row with the most stars shows the most. The Ruby row has 8 stars, so it shows 8 shells.

items.q: How many more books did Mia read than Oliver?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 1 book. Mia: 7 and Oliver: 3. How many more means find the difference: 7 − 3 = 4 books.

items.q: How many votes did Banana get?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 1 vote. The Banana row has 4 circles, so it shows 4 votes.
Look at the key: each star stands for 1 bird. Read every row: Magpie 7, Lorikeet 4, Ibis 8, Kookaburra 5. Add them: 7 + 4 + 8 + 5 = 24 birds.

items.q: How many ice blocks were sold on Thursday?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 2 ice blocks. The Thu row has 4 squares: 4 × 2 = 8 ice blocks.

items.q: How many students ride a bike to school?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 2 students. The Bike row has 4 circles and half a circle: 4 × 2 = 8, and half of 2 is 1, so 8 + 1 = 9 students.
The key says one whole star = 2 votes. Half a star is half of 2, which is 1 vote.

items.q: Each star stands for 2 books. Noah read 12 books. How many stars should be in his row?
items.e: Count in 2s until you reach 12: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. That is 6 steps, so draw 6 stars. Check: 6 × 2 = 12. (Drawing 12 stars would show 12 × 2.)

items.q: Which row shows 9 students?
items.e: Half a circle is 1, so 9 students is 4 and a half circles. The Soccer row has 4 circles and half a circle: 4 × 2 = 8, and half of 2 is 1, so 8 + 1 = 9 students.
Look at the key: each star stands for 2 birds. The Lorikeet row has 5 stars and half a star: 5 × 2 = 10, and half of 2 is 1, so 10 + 1 = 11 birds.

items.q: Which row shows the fewest books?
items.e: Every square stands for the same number, so the row with the fewest squares shows the fewest. The Oliver row has 1 square: 1 × 2 = 2 books.

items.q: How many more students walk to school than come by bus?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 2 students. Walk: 5 × 2 = 10 and Bus: 2 × 2 = 4. How many more means find the difference: 10 − 4 = 6 students.
Look at the key: each star stands for 5 cans. The 3C row has 3 stars: 3 × 5 = 15 cans.

items.q: Each square stands for 5 students. 35 students walk to school. How many squares should be in the Walk row?
items.e: Count in 5s until you reach 35: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. That is 7 steps, so draw 7 squares. Check: 7 × 5 = 35. (Drawing 35 squares would show 35 × 5.)

items.q: Which row shows 25 points?
items.e: Each circle = 5. 25 ÷ 5 = 5, so look for 5 circles. The Waratah row has 5 circles: 5 × 5 = 25 points.
Look at the key: each star stands for 5 votes. The Wombat row has 1 star: 1 × 5 = 5 votes.

items.q: Which row shows the most ice blocks?
items.e: Every square stands for the same number, so the row with the most squares shows the most. The Mon row has 4 squares: 4 × 5 = 20 ice blocks.

items.q: How many more votes did Orange get than Watermelon?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 5 votes. Orange: 2 × 5 = 10 and Watermelon: 1 × 5 = 5. How many more means find the difference: 10 − 5 = 5 votes.
Look at the key: each star stands for 5 cans. Read every row: 3A 25, 3B 15, 3C 30, 3D 20. Add them: 25 + 15 + 30 + 20 = 90 cans.

sets.title: Column graphs with scales of 1, 2 and 5

items.q: How many families have 5 people?
items.e: The scale goes up in 1s. The column for 5 people ends on the line for 4. So the answer is 4 families.

items.q: What does the scale on this column graph go up in?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 1, 2, 3 … Each line is 1 more than the one before, so the scale goes up in 1s.

items.q: Which column shows the most families?
items.e: The column for 4 people is the tallest one. The column for 4 people ends on the line for 7. It shows 7 families.

items.q: How many students have a dog?
items.e: The scale goes up in 1s. The column for Dog ends on the line for 6. So the answer is 6 students.

items.q: Which column shows 3 shells?
items.e: The scale goes up in 1s. Find 3 on the scale. The column for Ruby ends on the line for 3.

items.q: How many more votes did Watermelon get than Banana?
items.e: The scale goes up in 1s. Watermelon: 4. Banana: 2. How many more means find the difference: 4 − 2 = 2 votes.

items.q: What does the scale on this column graph go up in?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 2, 4, 6 … Each line is 2 more than the one before, so the scale goes up in 2s.

items.q: How many shells did Kai find?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. The column for Kai ends on the line for 12. So the answer is 12 shells.

items.q: How many students chose swimming?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. The column for Swimming ends halfway between 8 and 10, so it shows 9. So the answer is 9 students.

items.q: How many books did Isla read?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. The column for Isla ends halfway between 4 and 6, so it shows 5. So the answer is 5 books.

items.q: Which column shows 7 birds?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. Find 7 on the scale. The column for Magpie ends halfway between 6 and 8, so it shows 7.

items.q: Which column shows the fewest students?
items.e: The column for Car is the shortest one. The column for Car ends on the line for 2. It shows 2 students.

items.q: How many ice blocks were sold on Thursday?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. The column for Thu ends halfway between 8 and 10, so it shows 9. So the answer is 9 ice blocks.

items.q: How many more votes did the platypus get than the echidna?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. Platypus: 11. Echidna: 5. How many more means find the difference: 11 − 5 = 6 votes.

items.q: How many points did Waratah House get?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. The column for Waratah ends on the line for 25. So the answer is 25 points.

items.q: What does the scale on this column graph go up in?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 5, 10, 15 … Each line is 5 more than the one before, so the scale goes up in 5s.

items.q: How many points did Wattle House get?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. The column for Wattle ends on the line for 5. So the answer is 5 points.

items.q: Which column shows 20 ice blocks?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. Find 20 on the scale. The column for Mon ends on the line for 20.

items.q: How many more students ride a bike to school than walk?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. Bike: 30. Walk: 5. How many more means find the difference: 30 − 5 = 25 students.

items.q: How many votes did Apple and Banana get altogether?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. Apple: 20. Banana: 35. Altogether means add: 20 + 35 = 55 votes.

sets.title: Compare different graphs of the same data

items.q: Favourite colour (frequency table): Red 5, Blue 8, Pink 3, Grey 6. Which column graph shows the same data?
items.e: C matches every number (the scale goes up in 1s). A: two columns are the wrong way round; B: one column is one line too high; D: one column is one line too low.

items.q: People in families (frequency table): 2 people: 4, 3 people: 9, 4 people: 12, 5 people: 7. Which column graph shows the same data?
items.e: A matches every number (the scale goes up in 2s). B: two columns are the wrong way round; C: a column is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); D: one column is one line too high.

items.q: Cans collected (frequency table): 3A 25, 3B 40, 3C 15, 3D 30. Which column graph shows the same data?
items.e: D matches every number (the scale goes up in 5s). A: two columns are the wrong way round; B: one column is one line too high; C: one column is one line too low.

items.q: Ice blocks sold (frequency table): Mon 11, Tue 6, Wed 14, Thu 9. Which column graph shows the same data?
items.e: B matches every number (the scale goes up in 2s). A: two columns are the wrong way round; C: a column is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); D: one column is one line too high.
First count the tallies: Dog 6, Cat 4, Fish 3, Bird 5. B matches every number (each symbol = 1). A: two rows are the wrong way round; C: one row has a symbol too many; D: one row is missing a symbol.
D matches every number (each symbol = 2). A: two rows are the wrong way round; B: a half symbol is drawn as a whole symbol; C: one row has a symbol too many.
A matches every number (each symbol = 5). B: two rows are the wrong way round; C: one row has a symbol too many; D: one row is missing a symbol.

First count the tallies: Apple 10, Kiwi 7, Plum 12, Pear 5. C matches every number (each symbol = 2). A: two rows are the wrong way round; B: a half symbol is drawn as a whole symbol; D: one row has a symbol too many.

items.q: Which list of numbers matches this column graph? The numbers are in this order: AFL, cricket, netball, soccer.
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. The column for AFL ends on the line for 12. The column for Cricket ends halfway between 6 and 8, so it shows 7. The column for Netball ends on the line for 10. The column for Soccer ends halfway between 4 and 6, so it shows 5. Reading the columns that end between lines as the line below gives 12, 6, 10, 4.

items.q: Which list of numbers matches this column graph? The numbers are in this order: koala, kangaroo, wombat, echidna.
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. The column for Koala ends on the line for 30. The column for Kangaroo ends on the line for 15. The column for Wombat ends on the line for 25. The column for Echidna ends on the line for 10. Counting grid spaces instead of reading the scale gives 6, 3, 5, 2.

items.q: Which list of numbers matches this column graph? The numbers are in this order: magpies, galahs, lorikeets, ibises.
items.e: The scale goes up in 1s. The column for Magpie ends on the line for 6. The column for Galah ends on the line for 9. The column for Lorikeet ends on the line for 4. The column for Ibis ends on the line for 7. Read the line at the top of each column, not the space above it.

items.q: The pictograph and the column graph show the same data. How many votes should the missing Banana column show?
items.e: Read the Banana row of the pictograph. Each circle = 2 votes. The Banana row has 4 circles and half a circle: 4 × 2 = 8, and half of 2 is 1, so 8 + 1 = 9 votes. Draw the Banana column up to 9.
Read the Zara row of the pictograph. Each star = 5 shells. The Zara row has 5 stars: 5 × 5 = 25 shells. Draw the Zara column up to 25.

items.q: The pictograph and the column graph show the same data. How many books should the missing Noah column show?
items.e: Read the Noah row of the pictograph. Each square = 1 book. The Noah row has 6 squares, so it shows 6 books. Draw the Noah column up to 6.

items.q: The pictograph and the column graph show the same data. How many students should the missing Bus column show?
items.e: Read the Bus row of the pictograph. Each circle = 2 students. The Bus row has 3 circles and half a circle: 3 × 2 = 6, and half of 2 is 1, so 6 + 1 = 7 students. Draw the Bus column up to 7.

items.q: How many more students in Class 3B than in Class 3A have a cat?
items.e: Class 3B cat: 8. Class 3A cat: 5. How many more means subtract: 8 − 5 = 3.

items.q: Which pet is the most common in Class 3A but not in Class 3B?
items.e: In Class 3A the tallest column is Dog (7). In Class 3B the tallest column is Cat (8).

items.q: How many students in the two classes have a bird?
items.e: Class 3A bird: 4. Class 3B bird: 6. Both classes means add: 4 + 6 = 10.

items.q: How many students are shown in Class 3B’s graph?
items.e: Add the Class 3B columns: 4 + 8 + 3 + 6 = 21. (18 is Class 3A: 7 + 5 + 2 + 4.)

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: Both classes have the same number of dogs.
Class 3B has 1 more fish than Class 3A.
Class 3A has more cats than Class 3B.
items.e: Fish: Class 3B 3, Class 3A 2, so 3B has 1 more. Class 3A has 5 cats and 3B has 8. Dogs: 7 and 4. Class 3A has 4 birds; 6 birds is Class 3B.

items.q: How many students chose AFL or soccer?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. AFL ends on 12. Soccer ends halfway between 8 and 10, so 9. AFL or soccer means add: 12 + 9 = 21. (Reading soccer as 8 gives 20.)

items.q: How many more students chose netball than swimming?
items.e: Netball 10, swimming 4. How many more means subtract: 10 − 4 = 6. (14 is the sum, and 3 counts the grid spaces between the columns.)

items.q: Every student in Year 3 voted once. How many students voted?
items.e: Read every column: 12, 7, 10, 9 and 4. Cricket and soccer end between gridlines, so they are 7 and 9. 12 + 7 + 10 + 9 + 4 = 42. (Reading 7 and 9 as 6 and 8 gives 40.)

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: Soccer got more votes than netball.
Cricket got 3 more votes than swimming.
Swimming was the most popular sport.
AFL got twice as many votes as netball.
items.e: Cricket 7 and swimming 4: 7 − 4 = 3, so this is true. Soccer (9) is less than netball (10). Swimming (4) is the least popular. Twice netball would be 20, not 12.

items.q: The teacher will choose the two most popular sports for the next sport lesson. Which two?
items.e: The two tallest columns are AFL (12) and netball (10). Soccer is 9, just below netball.

items.q: How many pieces of fruit were eaten at recess altogether?
items.e: Each circle = 2, so half a circle = 1. Apple 8, banana 5 × 2 + 1 = 11, mango 6, orange 2 × 2 + 1 = 5. 8 + 11 + 6 + 5 = 30. (Counting the circles gives 16. Leaving out the halves gives 28.)

items.q: How many more bananas than oranges were eaten?
items.e: Banana 11, orange 5. How many more means subtract: 11 − 5 = 6. (3 is the difference in the number of circles, not in pieces of fruit.)

items.q: Ice blocks cost $2 each. How much money did the canteen make from ice blocks on Thursday?
items.e: Thursday: 35 ice blocks. Each costs $2, so 35 × 2 = 70. The canteen made $70. (35 is the number of ice blocks, not dollars.)

items.q: On which day were 15 more ice blocks sold than on Wednesday?
items.e: Wednesday: 10. 15 more than 10 is 10 + 15 = 25. Tuesday shows 25. (Monday shows 15, but the question asks for 15 more than Wednesday.)

items.q: On two days the weather was very hot. Which two days were most likely the hot days?
items.e: People buy more ice blocks on hot days. The two tallest columns are Thursday (35) and Friday (40).

items.q: How many students do not come to school by car?
items.e: Not by car means walk, bus or bike: 9 + 6 + 3 = 18. (32 is everyone, and 14 is only the car students.)

items.q: Next week 5 of the car students will walk instead. How many students will walk?
items.e: 5 more students will walk: 9 + 5 = 14. (19 adds the 5 to the car row instead.)

items.q: What is the most common number of people in a family?
items.e: The tallest column is above 4, so 4 people is the most common. The column is 8 high, which means 8 families, not 8 people.

items.q: How many families have 5 or more people?
items.e: 5 or more means the columns for 5 and 6 people: 4 + 2 = 6 families. (11 adds the family sizes 5 + 6, not the families.)

items.q: How many families were in the survey?
items.e: Add the heights of all the columns: 3 + 6 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 23 families. (20 adds the numbers under the columns, 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6.)

items.q: Year 3 wants to collect 150 cans. How many more cans do they need?
items.e: Each square = 5 cans. 3A 30, 3B 45, 3C 20, 3D 35. Step 1: 30 + 45 + 20 + 35 = 130. Step 2: 150 − 130 = 20. (Counting squares gives 26, and 150 − 26 = 124.)

items.q: Class 3B says, “We collected more cans than 3A and 3C together.” Are they right?
c: No. 3A and 3C collected 50, which is 5 more.
items.e: 3B: 9 squares × 5 = 45 cans. 3A and 3C together: 30 + 20 = 50 cans. 50 is more than 45, so 3B is wrong.

items.q: Mia is drawing a column graph. The scale goes up in 2s. Netball got 7 votes. Where should the top of the netball column be?
items.e: There is no line for 7, because the lines go 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. 7 is halfway between 6 and 8. (The 7th line up is 14.)

items.q: Leo will draw a pictograph of 10, 15, 20 and 5 votes. He wants whole symbols only and as few symbols as he can. Which key should he use?
items.e: Every number is in the 5 times table, so a key of 5 gives whole symbols: 2, 3, 4 and 1. A key of 10 would need half symbols for 15 and 5. Keys of 1 or 2 need many more symbols.

items.q: How many more students chose netball or soccer than chose AFL?
items.e: Step 1: netball or soccer: 10 + 9 = 19. Step 2: AFL is 12. 19 − 12 = 7 more. (31 adds all three. 3 is 12 − 9.)
